content: Any paper sources that will be followed?

For the first couple of steps (getting the explicit solutions and solvability in Schwartz space), I think the PDE book by Rauch is pretty good for the intuition. I guess for the proofs it always is a good idea to look into Hörmander.
When we get to nontrivial results about dispersive equations such as Strichartz estimates, there is obviously the famous Keel-Tao paper, the book by Cazenave on semilinear Schrödinger and Tao's book on dispersive PDEs. One of my goals is to be able to prove the non-endpoint Strichartz estimates (and maybe a simple existence result from NLS derived from that), which I think is very much in reach. If there is significant interest, then I am happy to look into more challenging topics (more complicated spaces, more precise estimates)..

I'm wondering if it's feasible to try to fold in the project some aspect of making various constants explicit, in a manner similar to what has been proposed for analytic number theory? Or is that too much of a side-quest?

Yes, I also have the impression that having a computer help you keep track of certain quantities should be really helpful in this area. My recollection from learning a bit about this topic was that there were a lot of calculations that were basically about finding the right sets of exponents for various Hölder/Strichartz/Sobolev estimates to make an iteration scheme work. If it is possible to put these ingredients in a form that some old-school AI system can find a solution I think that would be amazing.

I will be able to actually write some code in starting after next week, but if someone else wants to start here would be things work on (or just even discuss the right approach): the Gaussian as a Schwartz function and the derivative of a function from the reals to a locally convex TVS (aka PolynormableSpace or WithSeminorms).

The first one is needed for the explicit representation of the solution operator for Schrödinger (one needs an imaginary Gaussian, which is only a tempered distribution but as such can still be Fourier transformed). The second one is to show that the Fourier multiplier representation does solve the equation (one needs to be able to calculate time derivatives for that obviously).

I've added some simple projects at https://github.com/mcdoll/DispersiveEquations/issues?q=sort%3Aupdated-desc+is%3Aissue+state%3Aopen+ and https://mcdoll.github.io/DispersiveEquations/ (now with references!)
I am always happy to go into more detail if someone is interested in working on any of these, but intimidated by the maths or the Lean formalization.
